header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Park (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Ava Martinez (Helm Capital, Head of ML), Noah Singh (Helm, VP Eng), Rachel Kim (Helm, FinOps)
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Sofia, I'm the account exec for this region. Quick check, audio good?
[00:09] Ava (Helm): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks, Sofia.
[00:12] Liam (Redwood SE): Hi all, Liam from Redwood infra, I'll focus on the perf/cost bits today.
[00:16] Noah (Helm): Great, we have about 45 minutes, want to focus on unit economics — per-token, batching, caching, and whether Hosted or Dedicated makes sense for us.
[00:27] Sofia: Perfect. To set context, can you share a little about your workload? QPS, payload sizes, and budget constraints?
[00:36] Ava: Sure. We run customer-facing summarization and alerting. Typical prompt plus history is around 1.2k tokens, sometimes up to 3k. Peak QPS is 40, avg 12. We want latency under 400ms P95 for the short prompts, but okay to degrade for longer ones. Budget — roughly $12k/month target initially.
[00:56] Liam: Cool. With those numbers we usually look at two levers: batching/batch windows and prefix/KV caching to lower per-token compute. For hosted per-token pricing, we have base rates and then reserved capacity discounts if you commit.
[01:10] Rachel (FinOps): Can you clarify how batching affects latency? If we batch more we get lower cost, but that will add latency, right?
[01:17] Liam: Exactly. There's tradeoff. For QPS ~40 bursts, you can do micro-batching with 5–20ms aggregation and still keep P95 under your 400ms target for short prompts. Larger batch windows (100–200ms) cut cost more but push latency up. Also KV caching — if many requests share prefixes, you avoid recomputing early tokens.
[01:35] Ava: Our traffic is 70% similar templates, so prefix caching sounds promising. Are there any restrictions on cache staleness or consistency?
[01:41] Liam: Good q—cache is best-effort for identical prefixes. For stateful contexts or user-specific privacy concerns, you can scope caches per-tenant or disable for sensitive flows. We expose TTL and size knobs.
[01:52] Noah: For Dedicated, how big is the uplift vs Hosted? Our expectation is you get better unit economics when you reserve GPUs but there's a minimum commit.
[02:00] Sofia: Right. Hosted is simple usage-based billing — pay-per-token. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools; you get a lower per-token compute cost but you pay for committed capacity. We can model both against your QPS to find breakeven. Typical breakeven for CPU-bound-ish workloads is around X tokens/month — sorry, let me pull numbers — (paper rustling) — for a single A100-equivalent pool, customers see ~30–45% lower per-token compute, depends on utilization.
[02:25] Rachel: What about Private/VPC? We might need that later for audit controls. Does that change pricing?
[02:29] Liam: Private deployments add platform and support fees; the variant for on-prem has higher fixed costs but you get full isolation. For cost-econ, it behaves like Dedicated plus infra ops overhead.
[02:39] Ava: Our main question is: can we hit the $12k/mo target with acceptable latency? Give us a back-of-envelope.
[02:45] Liam: Quick calc — assume avg tokens per request 1.2k, avg 12 QPS -> roughly 1.04M tokens/hour, ~25M tokens/day, ~750M tokens/month. At hosted list price of $0.00002 per token (example), that's $15k/mo — that's already above $12k. But with caching that reduces to effective tokens by say 40% you get to ~9k. With batching/reserved discounts could reach target.
[03:14] Noah: Wait, that per-token price seems high compared to what we've seen with other providers. Are you comparing input+output tokens?
[03:20] Sofia: Good call; we bill based on input+output tokens. Some competitors only list output or have different counting. We'll send the annotated pricing sheet.
[03:27] Rachel: Also curious about quantization options — does Redwood provide lower-precision model variants to reduce cost?
[03:31] Liam: Yes, we support quantized model variants and the runtime picks kernels. For many transformer models, 4-bit quant yields similar generation quality and halves memory and sometimes improves throughput, depending on kernel availability. That helps both Hosted and Dedicated.
[03:46] Ava: Do you do automatic model routing or would we need to change calls to switch variants?
[03:50] Liam: We have smart routing: policy-based. You can route by latency SLO, cost tier, or region, and the runtime will pick compatible variants. For a pilot we can route low-cost traffic to quantized variants and keep high-SLA to full-precision.
[04:03] Noah: For the pilot, we'd want to run on our sample workload and compare latency and cost for Hosted vs Dedicated. What's the typical pilot setup?
[04:12] Sofia: Usually we do a 2-week pilot: one week of benchmarking in our hosted env using your payloads, then an optional dedicated trial where we provision a small reserved pool for a week. We'll produce a cost model and a side-by-side perf report.
[04:25] Ava: Sounds good. Any procurement/legal blockers we should expect for Hosted? SSO/SAML, SOC2?
[04:31] Sofia: We have SOC 2 type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs and KMS integrations. For Private we offer Customer-managed KMS/HSM. I'll attach our security datasheet.
[04:42] Rachel: Billing cadence — monthly invoice? Do you support committed spend discounts and true-up?
[04:46] Sofia: Yes monthly invoicing. For Dedicated we do committed monthly/annual contracts with true-up options and a discount ladder based on utilization.
[04:54] Noah: Back to the numbers — can you quantify the batching gain? If we micro-batch to 8 reqs per batch what's the token cost reduction?
[05:01] Liam: Token compute doesn't change but GPU utilization improves: latency per token goes down when you amortize attention kernel overhead across more sequences. In practice we see 20–40% cost-per-token savings from batching when sequence lengths are small to medium. For long sequences the marginal benefit decreases.
[05:20] Ava: We have many long sequences too — up to 3k tokens. How does KV cache interact with long sequences?
[05:25] Liam: KV caching stores past activations so repeats or conversational history avoids recomputing the early tokens. If your 3k sessions re-use a 1k opening prompt, the effective new tokens are 2k per request. That can be a big save. But for purely long unique prompts caching helps less.
[05:40] Rachel: Any recommended configuration to optimize within our $12k? Like reserved bursts plus caching?
[05:45] Liam: A common config: 50% reserved Dedicated pool scaled for peak bursts, plus hosted overflow; aggressive prefix caching (per-tenant), and quantized variants for non-critical flows. That usually slices 30–50% off list costs.
[05:58] Sofia: Also an operational note: we expose token-level cost telemetry in the console so you can see which routes or prompts are expensive and tune them.
[06:06] Ava: That visibility is important. Can the telemetry export to our FinOps tools?
[06:09] Sofia: Yes, we have CSV/JSON export and can integrate with billing webhook.
[06:15] Noah: Are there any hidden costs — egress, storage for KV cache, or logging?
[06:20] Liam: Good point. There's small storage for cache and logs in tiered pricing. Egress for large embeddings exports can add costs; we'll flag those. We'll include an itemized estimate in the pricing sheet.
[06:30] Ava: On security, we may need HIPAA-like controls for some customers later. How does Private compare?
[06:36] Sofia: Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you more control: customer-managed network, KMS, and audit log residency. That increases fixed cost but meets stricter reg requirements.
[06:45] Rachel: Procurement timeline: we need legal review and an SOW. Who on your side handles procurement?
[06:50] Sofia: I handle initial procurement; our legal ops will provide standard SOW and security exhibits. For Dedicated we'll coordinate finance for contract terms.
[06:58] Noah: Ok next step is the pilot. Ava will send sample payloads. Sofia and Liam will send pricing and benchmark docs.
[07:05] Ava: Yep I'll send by Monday. Quick question — you mentioned per-token price of $0.00002 earlier; can you send a worked example comparing Hosted vs Dedicated for our traffic?
[07:12] Sofia: Yes we'll run the back-of-envelope with your sample payloads. Expect a detailed spreadsheet that shows sensitivity to cache hit-rate, batching window, and quantization.
[07:21] Liam: Also note competitor differences — some vendors charge per request or have different token counting. We'll annotate.
[07:27] Rachel: And please include worst-case numbers so procurement can size contingencies.
[07:31] Sofia: Absolutely. Anything else?
[07:34] Ava: Not on my side. Thanks — that was helpful.
[07:37] Noah: Thanks everyone.
[07:39] Sofia: Great, we'll follow up with materials and propose pilot times. Bye.
[07:44] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript has mild transcription artifacts — e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash; Redwood Dedicated mis-typed in places. Speakers occasionally overlap; I left filler words and short crosstalk fragments to preserve realism. Reference artifacts mentioned: "pricing sheet (link)" and "benchmark spreadsheet (link)" — Redwood to attach in follow-up email.
